fields.Front: What are the two concrete node types in a Composite-pattern file system model, and what do they represent?
fields.Back: File (leaf — holds actual content/size, no children) and Directory (composite — holds a collection of child FileSystemNode objects, which may themselves be Files or Directories).

fields.Front: What common interface/abstract class do File and Directory both implement in the Composite pattern, and what methods does it declare?
fields.Back: FileSystemNode (or Node), declaring at minimum getName(), getSize(), and often getParent() — so client code can treat files and directories uniformly.

fields.Front: Why does Directory need a reference to its parent node?
fields.Back: To support operations like computing the absolute path, moving up the tree, or validating a move doesn't create a cycle (can't move a directory into its own descendant).

fields.Front: In the File System design, which class owns the list of child nodes, and what data structure is typical?
fields.Back: Directory owns the children, typically a Map<String, FileSystemNode> keyed by name for O(1) lookup, or a List if insertion order matters.

fields.Front: Why is the Composite pattern the natural fit for a file system's File/Directory relationship?
fields.Back: Operations like getSize(), delete(), or print() need to work identically whether called on a single file or an entire directory subtree — Composite lets Directory's implementation just delegate to each child polymorphically, without the caller knowing which type it's dealing with.

fields.Front: Besides Composite, what pattern would you add to support new cross-cutting operations (search, compress, count-by-extension) without modifying File/Directory classes?
fields.Back: The Visitor pattern: define a FileSystemVisitor interface with visit(File) and visit(Directory) methods, and have each node call accept(visitor) — new operations become new Visitor implementations instead of new methods on every node class.

fields.Front: How would the Decorator pattern apply to a file system that supports optional compression or encryption on files?
fields.Back: Wrap a File in a CompressedFile or EncryptedFile decorator implementing the same FileSystemNode interface, so behavior (e.g. read/write transforms the bytes) is added transparently without subclassing every combination.

fields.Front: What is the classic recursive-size edge case for a Directory.getSize() implementation, and why does naive recursion risk infinite loops?
fields.Back: Symbolic links (symlinks) that point back up the tree (or to themselves) create cycles; naive recursion following every child recurses forever. Fix: track visited node IDs/inodes and skip already-visited nodes, or don't follow symlinks by default.

fields.Front: Why should deleting a non-empty Directory require either a recursive/force flag or fail by default?
fields.Back: Silently deleting all descendants is destructive and surprising; APIs typically mirror real file systems by requiring an explicit recursive=true flag (like rm -r) or throwing an exception if the directory isn't empty.

fields.Front: What edge case arises from case sensitivity when adding a child to a Directory (e.g. adding 'Notes.txt' when 'notes.txt' exists)?
fields.Back: Behavior differs by target OS: case-sensitive file systems (Linux) allow both to coexist as distinct files, case-insensitive ones (Windows/macOS default) must treat them as the same name and reject/overwrite — the design should make this policy explicit and configurable.

fields.Front: Should FileSystem.getSize(directory) compute size eagerly (cached, updated on every write) or lazily (recomputed on each call)? What's the tradeoff?
fields.Back: Eager/cached: O(1) reads but every write must propagate size deltas up to every ancestor. Lazy: O(1) writes but O(n) reads (full subtree walk). Most designs cache and propagate deltas upward since size reads are far more frequent than the propagation cost.

fields.Front: What API method would let a client move a directory, and what validation must it perform before allowing the move?
fields.Back: move(FileSystemNode node, Directory newParent) — must reject the move if newParent is node itself or a descendant of node (that would detach the tree into a cycle).

fields.Front: What API method lists a directory's immediate contents, and why should it not recurse by default?
fields.Back: List<FileSystemNode> listChildren(Directory dir) — returning only immediate children (not the full recursive tree) keeps the call cheap and predictable; recursive listing should be a separate, explicit operation (e.g. via a Visitor).

fields.Front: Java: implement the Composite pattern with an abstract FileSystemNode, a File leaf, and a Directory composite whose getSize() sums its children.
fields.Back:
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

abstract class FileSystemNode {
    protected String name;
    protected Directory parent;

    public FileSystemNode(String name) { this.name = name; }
    public abstract long getSize();
    public String getName() { return name; }
}

class File extends FileSystemNode {
    private long sizeInBytes;

    public File(String name, long sizeInBytes) {
        super(name);
        this.sizeInBytes = sizeInBytes;
    }

    @Override
    public long getSize() { return sizeInBytes; }
}

class Directory extends FileSystemNode {
    private final Map<String, FileSystemNode> children = new HashMap<>();

    public Directory(String name) { super(name); }

    public void add(FileSystemNode node) {
        node.parent = this;
        children.put(node.getName(), node);
    }

    @Override
    public long getSize() {
        long total = 0;
        for (FileSystemNode child : children.values()) {
            total += child.getSize();
        }
        return total;
    }
}

fields.Front: Python: write a recursive get_size(node, visited=None) function that computes a directory tree's total size while avoiding infinite recursion from symlink cycles.
fields.Back:
def get_size(node, visited=None):
    if visited is None:
        visited = set()
    if id(node) in visited:
        return 0
    visited.add(id(node))

    if node.is_file:
        return node.size_bytes

    return sum(get_size(child, visited) for child in node.children.values())

fields.Front: Java: implement a depth-first findByName(Directory root, String targetName) search over a file system tree, returning the first matching node or null.
fields.Back:
public FileSystemNode findByName(Directory root, String targetName) {
    if (root.getName().equals(targetName)) {
        return root;
    }
    for (FileSystemNode child : root.getChildren()) {
        if (child.getName().equals(targetName)) {
            return child;
        }
        if (child instanceof Directory) {
            FileSystemNode found = findByName((Directory) child, targetName);
            if (found != null) {
                return found;
            }
        }
    }
    return null;
}

fields.Front: Python: implement Directory.add_child(node) that raises if a child with the same name already exists.
fields.Back:
class Directory(FileSystemNode):
    def __init__(self, name):
        super().__init__(name)
        self.children = {}

    def add_child(self, node):
        if node.name in self.children:
            raise FileExistsError(f"'{node.name}' already exists in '{self.name}'")
        node.parent = self
        self.children[node.name] = node

fields.Text: A file system's core requirements include: {{c1::create}} files/directories, {{c2::delete}} them, {{c3::move/rename}} them, {{c4::list}} a directory's contents, and compute {{c5::size}} recursively.
The {{c1::NodeType}} enum distinguishes {{c2::FILE}} from {{c3::DIRECTORY}} when Composite polymorphism alone isn't enough (e.g. for serialization or a switch in client code).

fields.Back: Structural pattern that lets you compose objects into tree structures and treat individual objects (leaves) and compositions of objects (composites) uniformly through a shared interface.
